claim: The UK Biobank study included 117,698 participants with 4,658 glaucoma cases and 113,040 controls.
source: Using 4,658 glaucoma cases and 113,040 controls in a cross-sectional study of the UK Biobank, we investigated whether plasma metabolites enhanced glaucoma prediction and if a metabolomic signature of resilience in high-genetic-risk individuals existed.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample sizes in the abstract and these numbers are confirmed in the results section and Figure 1.

claim: Metabolites weakly predicted glaucoma with an Area Under the Curve of 0.579.
source: While metabolites weakly predicted glaucoma (Area Under the Curve = 0.579), they offered marginal prediction improvement in PRS-only-based models (p=0.004).
evidence: The AUC value is directly reported in the abstract and supported by Figure 3 showing ROC curves.

claim: Metabolites offered marginal prediction improvement in PRS-only-based models with p=0.004.
source: While metabolites weakly predicted glaucoma (Area Under the Curve = 0.579), they offered marginal prediction improvement in PRS-only-based models (p=0.004).
evidence: The p-value is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis described in the results.

claim: Elevated lactate levels (p=8.8E-12) were linked to reduced glaucoma prevalence in the top PRS decile.
source: We identified a metabolomic signature associated with resilience in the top glaucoma PRS decile, with elevated glycolysis-related metabolites—lactate (p=8.8E-12), pyruvate (p=1.9E-10), and citrate (p=0.02)—linked to reduced glaucoma prevalence.
evidence: The p-value for lactate is explicitly stated in the abstract and confirmed in Table 5.

claim: Elevated pyruvate levels (p=1.9E-10) were linked to reduced glaucoma prevalence in the top PRS decile.
source: We identified a metabolomic signature associated with resilience in the top glaucoma PRS decile, with elevated glycolysis-related metabolites—lactate (p=8.8E-12), pyruvate (p=1.9E-10), and citrate (p=0.02)—linked to reduced glaucoma prevalence.
evidence: The p-value for pyruvate is explicitly stated in the abstract and confirmed in Table 5.

claim: Elevated citrate levels (p=0.02) were linked to reduced glaucoma prevalence in the top PRS decile.
source: We identified a metabolomic signature associated with resilience in the top glaucoma PRS decile, with elevated glycolysis-related metabolites—lactate (p=8.8E-12), pyruvate (p=1.9E-10), and citrate (p=0.02)—linked to reduced glaucoma prevalence.
evidence: The p-value for citrate is explicitly stated in the abstract and confirmed in Table 5.

claim: Lactate, pyruvate, and citrate combined significantly modified the PRS-glaucoma relationship with Pinteraction = 0.011.
source: These metabolites combined significantly modified the PRS-glaucoma relationship (Pinteraction = 0.011).
evidence: The interaction p-value is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by Figure 5.

claim: Higher total resilience metabolite levels within the highest PRS quartile corresponded to lower glaucoma prevalence with an odds ratio of 0.71 (95% CI = 0.64–0.80).
source: Higher total resilience metabolite levels within the highest PRS quartile corresponded to lower glaucoma prevalence (Odds Ratiohighest vs. lowest total resilience metabolite quartile=0.71, 95% Confidence Interval = 0.64–0.80).
evidence: The odds ratio and confidence interval are explicitly stated in the abstract and confirmed in Figure 5B.

claim: Dietary pyruvate mitigated elevated intraocular pressure (p=0.002) in Lmx1bV265D mice.
source: Dietary pyruvate mitigated elevated intraocular pressure (p=0.002) and optic nerve damage (p<0.0003) in Lmx1bV265D mice.
evidence: The p-value for IOP reduction is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by Figure 7C.

claim: Dietary pyruvate mitigated optic nerve damage (p<0.0003) in Lmx1bV265D mice.
source: Dietary pyruvate mitigated elevated intraocular pressure (p=0.002) and optic nerve damage (p<0.0003) in Lmx1bV265D mice.
evidence: The p-value for optic nerve damage reduction is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by Figure 7D.

claim: Glaucoma is a polygenic, progressive neurodegenerative disease and a leading cause of irreversible blindness.
source: Glaucoma is a polygenic, progressive neurodegenerative disease and a leading cause of irreversible blindness (Soh et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Soh et al., 2021.

claim: Around 50 to 70% of people affected by glaucoma remain undiagnosed.
source: The disease is typically asymptomatic until advanced visual field loss occurs, and around 50 to 70% of people affected remain undiagnosed (Khawaja and Viswanathan, 2018; Jan et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Khawaja and Viswanathan, 2018 and Jan et al., 2024.

claim: Population-based glaucoma screening is not cost-effective from a public health perspective.
source: Early detection and intervention are essential to stop disease progression and prevent visual impairment in glaucoma-affected individuals, as there is no cure available; however, population-based glaucoma screening is not cost-effective from a public health perspective (Moyer, 2013; US Preventive Services Task Force, 2022; Zukerman et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Moyer, 2013; US Preventive Services Task Force, 2022; and Zukerman et al., 2021.

claim: Glaucoma was five times more likely in the UK Biobank among participants with the highest genetic risk decile versus the lowest decile (7.4 vs 1.3%).
source: Glaucoma was five times more likely in the UK Biobank (UKBB) among participants with the highest genetic risk decile versus the lowest decile (7.4 vs 1.3%) (Sekimitsu et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sekimitsu et al., 2023.

claim: UKBB participants were predominately of European ancestry (85.8%).
source: UKBB participants were predominately of European ancestry (85.8%) but were also of mixed American (0.22%), Asian (2.77%), and African (1.73%) ancestry.
evidence: The percentages are explicitly stated in the results section.

claim: Glaucoma cases were associated with male gender.
source: Notably, characteristics associated with glaucoma included male gender, older age, genetic African ancestry (see Privé et al., 2022 for the method to determine genetically inferred ancestry in the UKBB), prior history of smoking, slightly lower cholesterol levels, higher body mass index (BMI), higher hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), higher IOP, thinner macular retinal nerve fiber layer (mRNFL) thickness, higher caffeine intake, higher alcohol intake, higher oral steroid use, diabetes, and coronary artery disease.
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 showing significant differences in sex distribution between glaucoma cases and controls (p<0.001).

claim: Glaucoma cases were associated with older age.
source: Notably, characteristics associated with glaucoma included male gender, older age, genetic African ancestry (see Privé et al., 2022 for the method to determine genetically inferred ancestry in the UKBB), prior history of smoking, slightly lower cholesterol levels, higher body mass index (BMI), higher hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), higher IOP, thinner macular retinal nerve fiber layer (mRNFL) thickness, higher caffeine intake, higher alcohol intake, higher oral steroid use, diabetes, and coronary artery disease.
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 showing mean age of 60.9 years for glaucoma cases vs 56.7 years for controls (p<0.001).

claim: Glaucoma cases were associated with higher intraocular pressure.
source: Notably, characteristics associated with glaucoma included male gender, older age, genetic African ancestry (see Privé et al., 2022 for the method to determine genetically inferred ancestry in the UKBB), prior history of smoking, slightly lower cholesterol levels, higher body mass index (BMI), higher hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), higher IOP, thinner macular retinal nerve fiber layer (mRNFL) thickness, higher caffeine intake, higher alcohol intake, higher oral steroid use, diabetes, and coronary artery disease.
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 showing mean IOP of 17.8 mmHg for glaucoma cases vs 15.9 mmHg for controls (p<0.001).

claim: The addition of 168 metabolites to Model 2 demonstrated the best performance with an AUC value of 0.670 compared to 0.664 without metabolites (p=0.002).
source: In model 2, the addition of the 168 metabolite panel demonstrated the best performance, with an AUC value of 0.670 (95% CI = 0.660–0.680) compared to 0.664 (95% CI = 0.654–0.674) for the model without metabolites (p=0.002) and 0.666 (95% CI = 0.656–0.676) for the limited panel of 27 metabolites.
evidence: The AUC values and p-value are explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3.

claim: In Model 4, the panel of 168 metabolites yielded the best performance with an AUC value of 0.806 compared to 0.801 without metabolites (p=0.004).
source: In model 4, the panel of 168 metabolites yielded the best performance with an AUC value of 0.806 (95% CI = 0.796–0.816), while the model without metabolites (AUC = 0.801, 95% CI = 0.791–0.811; p=0.004), as well as the model with a limited panel of 27 metabolites (AUC = 0.802, 95% CI = 0.792–0.812; p=0.006) both had lower AUC values.
evidence: The AUC values and p-value are explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3.

claim: Metabolites showed a modestly improved predictive value for glaucoma among people of White ethnicity (p<0.001).
source: Accordingly, we found that metabolites showed a modestly improved predictive value for glaucoma among people of White ethnicity (p<0.001), those aged 55 and older (p=0.002), and males (p=0.002) (Table 2).
evidence: The p-value is explicitly stated and supported by Table 2.

claim: Metabolites showed a modestly improved predictive value for glaucoma among those aged 55 and older (p=0.002).
source: Accordingly, we found that metabolites showed a modestly improved predictive value for glaucoma among people of White ethnicity (p<0.001), those aged 55 and older (p=0.002), and males (p=0.002) (Table 2).
evidence: The p-value is explicitly stated and supported by Table 2.

claim: Metabolites showed a modestly improved predictive value for glaucoma among males (p=0.002).
source: Accordingly, we found that metabolites showed a modestly improved predictive value for glaucoma among people of White ethnicity (p<0.001), those aged 55 and older (p=0.002), and males (p=0.002) (Table 2).
evidence: The p-value is explicitly stated and supported by Table 2.

claim: Higher probit-transformed levels of lactate (adjusted PNEF = 8.8E-12) were independently associated with no glaucoma in the top decile of glaucoma PRS.
source: Our multivariable-adjusted analysis revealed that higher probit-transformed levels of lactate (adjusted PNEF = 8.8E-12), pyruvate (adjusted PNEF = 2.9E-10), and citrate (adjusted PNEF = 0.018) were independently associated with no glaucoma in the top decile of glaucoma PRS (Table 5).
evidence: The adjusted p-value is explicitly stated and supported by Table 5.

claim: Higher probit-transformed levels of pyruvate (adjusted PNEF = 2.9E-10) were independently associated with no glaucoma in the top decile of glaucoma PRS.
source: Our multivariable-adjusted analysis revealed that higher probit-transformed levels of lactate (adjusted PNEF = 8.8E-12), pyruvate (adjusted PNEF = 2.9E-10), and citrate (adjusted PNEF = 0.018) were independently associated with no glaucoma in the top decile of glaucoma PRS (Table 5).
evidence: The adjusted p-value is explicitly stated and supported by Table 5.

claim: Higher probit-transformed levels of citrate (adjusted PNEF = 0.018) were independently associated with no glaucoma in the top decile of glaucoma PRS.
source: Our multivariable-adjusted analysis revealed that higher probit-transformed levels of lactate (adjusted PNEF = 8.8E-12), pyruvate (adjusted PNEF = 2.9E-10), and citrate (adjusted PNEF = 0.018) were independently associated with no glaucoma in the top decile of glaucoma PRS (Table 5).
evidence: The adjusted p-value is explicitly stated and supported by Table 5.

claim: A significant interaction was observed between elevated levels of total lactate, pyruvate, and citrate with glaucoma PRS quartile for predicting the risk of glaucoma (Pinteraction = 0.011).
source: Indeed, we observed a significant interaction between elevated levels of total lactate, pyruvate, and citrate with glaucoma PRS quartile for predicting the risk of glaucoma (Pinteraction = 0.011; Figure 5).
evidence: The interaction p-value is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 5.

claim: For individuals in PRS Q3 with total resilience-associated metabolite sum Q3, the glaucoma OR was 0.78 (95% CI = 0.65–0.93; p=0.0059).
source: For example, for individuals in PRS Q3 with total resilience-associated metabolite sum Q3, the glaucoma OR was 0.78 (95% CI = 0.65–0.93; p=0.0059), using metabolite sum Q1 as the reference.
evidence: The odds ratio, confidence interval, and p-value are explicitly stated and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: In PRS Q3 with a higher quartile of total resilience-associated metabolite sum (Q4), the OR was 0.74 (95% CI = 0.62–0.88; p=0.0009).
source: In the same PRS Q3 with a higher quartile of total resilience-associated metabolite sum (Q4), the OR was 0.74 (95% CI = 0.62–0.88; p=0.0009).
evidence: The odds ratio, confidence interval, and p-value are explicitly stated and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: The lowest OR of glaucoma was observed in participants with both the highest PRS (Q4) and highest resilience-associated metabolite sum (Q4), with an OR of 0.71 (95% CI = 0.64–0.80; p<0.001).
source: The lowest OR of glaucoma was observed in participants with both the highest PRS (Q4) and highest resilience-associated metabolite sum (Q4), with an OR of 0.71 (95% CI = 0.64–0.80; p<0.001).
evidence: The odds ratio, confidence interval, and p-value are explicitly stated and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: There was no evidence of a significant three-way interaction between the resilience-associated metabolite sum, PRS, and age (P3-way-interaction=0.65).
source: Although both age and PRS were significant predictors of glaucoma prevalence (both are strongly associated with increased risk), there was no evidence of a significant three-way interaction between the resilience-associated metabolite sum, PRS, and age (P3-way-interaction=0.65).
evidence: The three-way interaction p-value is explicitly stated.

claim: A significant interaction was found between glaucoma MRS built from 168 metabolites and PRS (Pinteraction = 0.0012).
source: We found a significant interaction between glaucoma MRS built from 168 metabolites and PRS (Pinteraction = 0.0012; see Appendix 2—figure 1A).
evidence: The interaction p-value is explicitly stated and supported by Appendix 2—figure 1A.

claim: Among individuals in the highest MRS quartile (Q4), PRS Q1 had an OR of 1.66 (95% CI = 1.15–2.42; p=0.0086).
source: Among individuals in the highest MRS quartile (Q4), PRS Q1 had an OR of 1.66 (95% CI = 1.15–2.42; p=0.0086), PRS Q2 had an OR of 2.08 (95% CI = 1.62–2.67; p<0.001), PRS Q3 had an OR of 2.20 (95% CI = 1.83–2.65; p<0.001), and PRS Q4 had an OR of 2.14 (95% CI = 1.91–2.40; p<0.001).
evidence: The odds ratio, confidence interval, and p-value are explicitly stated and supported by Appendix 2—figure 1B.

claim: Those with PRS Q4 (highest genetic risk) and MRS Q1 (lowest metabolic risk) had an OR of 11.7 (95% CI = 8.72–16.0; p<0.001) compared to PRS Q1 MRS Q1.
source: However, those with PRS Q4 (highest genetic risk) and MRS Q1 (lowest metabolic risk) had an OR of 11.7 (95% CI = 8.72–16.0; p<0.001) compared to PRS Q1 MRS Q1.
evidence: The odds ratio, confidence interval, and p-value are explicitly stated and supported by Figure 6B.

claim: The glaucoma OR increased to 25.1 (95% CI = 18.8–34.1; p<0.001) for those with PRS Q4, MRS Q4 (combination of highest genetic and highest metabolic risk; Pinteraction = 0.019).
source: Strikingly, the glaucoma OR further increased to 25.1 (95% CI = 18.8–34.1; p<0.001) for those with PRS Q4, MRS Q4 (combination of highest genetic and highest metabolic risk; Pinteraction = 0.019).
evidence: The odds ratio, confidence interval, and p-values are explicitly stated and supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Common variants in LMX1B are associated with IOP variation and primary open-angle glaucoma.
source: Common variants in LMX1B are associated with IOP variation and the most common form of human glaucoma, primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) (Choquet et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2018; Gharahkhani et al., 2021; Khawaja et al., 2018; MacGregor et al., 2018; Shiga et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rare Mendelian variants in LMX1B can produce early-onset ocular hypertension and open-angle glaucoma.
source: Rare Mendelian variants in LMX1B can produce early-onset ocular hypertension and open-angle glaucoma (OAG) (Cross et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cross et al., 2014.

claim: Mice with a dominant mutation in Lmx1b (Lmx1bV265D/+) develop IOP elevation and glaucoma.
source: We have previously demonstrated that mice with a dominant mutation in Lmx1b (Lmx1bV265D/+) develop IOP elevation and glaucoma (Cross et al., 2014; Tolman et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cross et al., 2014 and Tolman et al., 2021.

claim: Pyruvate supplementation substantially protected mice from IOP elevation.
source: Pyruvate supplementation through drinking water substantially protected mice from IOP elevation and glaucoma. Pyruvate significantly protected against both anterior chamber deepening (ACD), a consequence of IOP elevation in mouse eyes (Figure 7), and IOP elevation itself (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the text and Figure 7C showing IOP measurements with p=0.002.

claim: Pyruvate treatment protected against glaucomatous optic nerve degeneration.
source: Importantly, pyruvate treatment protected against glaucomatous optic nerve degeneration (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the text and Figure 7D showing optic nerve damage distributions with p<0.0003.

claim: The retina commonly utilizes energy produced from glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: The retina commonly utilizes energy produced from glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation. Therefore, glycolysis end products (pyruvate and lactate) are important energy sources for retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) (Williams and Casson, 2024)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Williams and Casson, 2024.

claim: RGCs express monocarboxylate transporters, which facilitate the uptake of extracellular pyruvate and lactate.
source: RGCs express monocarboxylate transporters, which facilitate the uptake of extracellular pyruvate and lactate, improving energy homeostasis, neuronal metabolism, and survival (Harun-Or-Rashid et al., 2020; Pappenhagen et al., 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Harun-Or-Rashid et al., 2020 and Pappenhagen et al., 2019.

claim: Lactate is critical for RGC survival during periods of glucose deprivation.
source: Lactate is critical for RGC survival during periods of glucose deprivation Vohra et al., 2019a; Rajala and Rajala, 2023 and bioenergetic insufficiency contributes to RGC loss in glaucoma (Williams et al., 2017b; Inman and Harun-Or-Rashid, 2017; Williams et al., 2017a; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Vohra et al., 2019a and Rajala and Rajala, 2023.

claim: Bioenergetic insufficiency contributes to RGC loss in glaucoma.
source: Lactate is critical for RGC survival during periods of glucose deprivation Vohra et al., 2019a; Rajala and Rajala, 2023 and bioenergetic insufficiency contributes to RGC loss in glaucoma (Williams et al., 2017b; Inman and Harun-Or-Rashid, 2017; Williams et al., 2017a; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2017b; Inman and Harun-Or-Rashid, 2017; Williams et al., 2017a; and Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Baseline lactate levels were significantly decreased in patients with normal-tension glaucoma compared to non-glaucomatous controls.
source: Finally, a study found that baseline lactate levels were significantly decreased in patients with normal-tension glaucoma compared to non-glaucomatous controls (Vohra et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vohra et al., 2019b.

claim: Pyruvate acts as an antioxidant, scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Beyond its metabolic functions, pyruvate also acts as an antioxidant, scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS), inducing the expression of the antioxidant response control gene Nrf2, and promoting beneficial autophagy (Jiménez-Moreno et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2013; Shin et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jiménez-Moreno et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2013; and Shin et al., 2012.

claim: Pyruvate's neuroprotective effects on RGCs have been demonstrated both in cell culture and in an induced model of glaucoma in rats.
source: Its neuroprotective effects on RGCs have been demonstrated both in cell culture and in an induced model of glaucoma in rats (Harder et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Harder et al., 2020.

claim: Pyruvate combined with nicotinamide has been shown to enhance optic nerve protection in mice.
source: Additionally, pyruvate combined with nicotinamide has been shown to enhance optic nerve protection in mice (Guymer et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guymer et al., 2018.

claim: A randomized phase II clinical trial found improved visual function in glaucoma patients treated with pyruvate and nicotinamide compared to the placebo group.
source: A randomized phase II clinical trial that tested pyruvate and nicotinamide in POAG patients found improved visual function in glaucoma patients compared to the placebo group (De Moraes et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to De Moraes et al., 2022.

claim: Lower plasma citrate levels have been found in glaucoma patients among adults and children.
source: Studies have found lower plasma citrate levels in glaucoma patients among adults and children (Fraenkl et al., 2011; Michalczuk et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fraenkl et al., 2011 and Michalczuk et al., 2017.

claim: A study measuring plasma citrate with a cutoff of 110 μmol/L to detect glaucoma had a sensitivity of 66.7% and a specificity of 71.4%.
source: A study measuring plasma citrate with a cutoff of 110  μmol/L to detect glaucoma had a sensitivity of 66.7% and a specificity of 71.4% (Fraenkl et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fraenkl et al., 2011.

claim: HDL has antioxidant properties to protect RGCs by facilitating cholesterol efflux from the retina.
source: Thus, HDL has antioxidant properties to protect RGCs by facilitating cholesterol efflux from the retina (Kelly et al., 2020; Morvaridzadeh et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kelly et al., 2020 and Morvaridzadeh et al., 2024.

claim: HDL analytes can cross blood-ocular barriers.
source: Furthermore, as HDL analytes can cross blood-ocular barriers (Hamel et al., 2024) there is a plausible route for serum-derived HDL to influence RGC homeostasis.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hamel et al., 2024.

claim: Genes implicated by large cross-ancestry and European subset GWAS meta-analyses of POAG risk are enriched in processes related to apolipoprotein binding and lipid transport.
source: Notably, genes implicated by large cross-ancestry and European subset GWAS meta-analyses of POAG risk are enriched in processes related to apolipoprotein binding and lipid transport (Gharahkhani et al., 2021; Hamel et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gharahkhani et al., 2021 and Hamel et al., 2024.

claim: The glaucoma PRS used in this study was from a multi-trait analysis of GWAS (MTAG) on glaucoma.
source: The glaucoma PRS used in this study was from a multi-trait analysis of GWAS (MTAG) on glaucoma (Craig et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Craig et al., 2020.

claim: The glaucoma PRS was constructed using single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with MTAG p-values ≤0.001, resulting in 2,673 uncorrelated SNPs after LD-clumping at r2=0.1.
source: The glaucoma PRS was constructed using single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with MTAG p-values ≤0.001, resulting in 2,673 uncorrelated SNPs after LD-clumping at r2=0.1, and was found to have a predictive ability with an AUC of 0.68 (95% confidence interval, CI, [0.67–0.70]) and 0.80 accounting for age, sex, family history, and PRS tested in the Australian and New Zealand Registry of Advanced Glaucoma cohort.
evidence: This statement is explicitly stated in the Methods section.

claim: The glaucoma PRS was found to have a predictive ability with an AUC of 0.68 (95% CI [0.67–0.70]) in the Australian and New Zealand Registry of Advanced Glaucoma cohort.
source: The glaucoma PRS was constructed using single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with MTAG p-values ≤0.001, resulting in 2,673 uncorrelated SNPs after LD-clumping at r2=0.1, and was found to have a predictive ability with an AUC of 0.68 (95% confidence interval, CI, [0.67–0.70]) and 0.80 accounting for age, sex, family history, and PRS tested in the Australian and New Zealand Registry of Advanced Glaucoma cohort.
evidence: This statement is explicitly stated in the Methods section and is supported by citation to Craig et al., 2020.

claim: The UK Biobank is a prospective cohort study of over half a million participants aged 37–73 years old at recruitment.
source: The UKBB is a prospective cohort study of over half a million participants aged 37–73 years old at recruitment across the United Kingdom from 2006 to 2010.
evidence: This statement is explicitly stated in the Methods section.

claim: A high-throughput nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)-based biomarker platform was used to measure the metabolomic profile in the UK Biobank.
source: In the UKBB, a high-throughput nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)-based biomarker platform (Nightingale Health Ltd; Helsinki, Finland) was used to measure the metabolomic profile in the randomly selected non-fasting EDTA plasma samples from a subset of participant. (Julkunen et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is explicitly stated in the Methods section and supported by a citation to Julkunen et al., 2021.

claim: The NMR platform contains data on 249 metabolic biomarkers (168 absolute levels and 81 ratio measures).
source: The NMR platform contains data on 249 metabolic biomarkers (168 absolute levels and 81 ratio measures), including a subset of 36 biomarkers (27 absolute levels and 9 ratio measures) certified for broad diagnostic use by the European Union (EU) (Julkunen et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is explicitly stated in the Methods section and supported by a citation to Julkunen et al., 2021.

claim: Pyruvate plays a central role in energy metabolism by linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle.
source: Pyruvate plays a central role in energy metabolism by linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle, ultimately driving ATP production by the electron transport chain.
evidence: This statement is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, which fuels the TCA cycle, and into lactate.
source: Pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, which fuels the TCA cycle, and into lactate, a key molecule that regulates metabolism and serves as an important energy source (Brooks, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brooks, 2020.

claim: The TCA cycle is tightly regulated to balance biosynthesis and energy production.
source: The TCA cycle is tightly regulated to balance biosynthesis (producing metabolic precursors for lipids, carbohydrates, amino acids, nucleic acids, and co-factors) and energy production, adjusting dynamically to cellular needs (Arnold and Finley, 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Arnold and Finley, 2023.

claim: Citrate is a key intermediate in the TCA cycle and is important for aerobic energy production.
source: Citrate is a key intermediate in the TCA cycle and is important for aerobic energy production.
evidence: This statement is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Elevated citrate levels might reflect enhanced energy supply and antioxidative capacity of ocular tissues.
source: Elevated citrate levels might reflect enhanced energy supply and antioxidative capacity of ocular tissues, potentially protecting RGCs against oxidative stress (Williams et al., 2017a; Wu et al., 2019; Morganti et al., 2020; Catalina-Rodriguez et al., 2012; Ohanele et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2017a; Wu et al., 2019; Morganti et al., 2020; Catalina-Rodriguez et al., 2012; and Ohanele et al., 2024.

claim: Decreased levels of citrate may indicate increased usage or mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Decreased levels of citrate may indicate increased usage or mitochondrial dysfunction (Chhimpa et al., 2023)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chhimpa et al., 2023.

claim: The prevalence of glaucoma in the UKBB sample (~4%) is similar to a directly performed disease burden estimate in a comparable United Kingdom sample (2.7%).
source: Nonetheless, it is reassuring that the prevalence of glaucoma in our sample (~4%) is similar to a directly performed disease burden estimate in a comparable, albeit slightly older, United Kingdom sample (2.7%) (Minassian et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Minassian et al., 2000.

claim: The addition of metabolite data marginally enhances the prediction of glaucoma beyond the use of demographic and genetic data.
source: Thus, these findings suggest that the addition of metabolite data marginally enhances the prediction of glaucoma beyond the use of demographic and genetic data.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the AUC comparisons presented in Figure 3 and the associated statistical tests.

claim: Pyruvate supplementation extends pyruvate's protective effects to the ocular drainage tissues, mitigating IOP elevation.
source: Importantly, the current study extends this evidence by demonstrating that pyruvate alone provides strong protection against glaucoma in a mouse model carrying a mutation in the ortholog of a human POAG gene. Furthermore, it extends pyruvate's protective effects to the ocular drainage tissues, mitigating IOP elevation.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results shown in Figure 7C demonstrating IOP reduction.

claim: The statistical interaction between metabolite scores and PRS-derived glaucoma risk helps identify individuals who, despite high genetic risk, are less likely to develop glaucoma due to favorable metabolic profiles.
source: The statistical interaction we demonstrate between metabolite scores and PRS-derived glaucoma risk helps identify individuals who, despite high genetic risk, are less likely to develop glaucoma due to favorable metabolic profiles or, on the contrary, are more likely to develop glaucoma and should be monitored at an earlier age.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interaction results presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: An MRS may provide clinically useful measures of metabolic status and improve patient risk stratification in glaucoma.
source: Overall, these findings indicate that an MRS may provide clinically useful measures of metabolic status and improve patient risk stratification in glaucoma.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the interaction analyses and predictive modeling results.

claim: A systematic review analyzing 13 studies identified a total of 144 metabolites, of which 12 were associated with OAG.
source: A systematic review analyzing 13 studies identified a total of 144 metabolites, of which 12 were associated with OAG (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Higher levels of plasma diglycerides and triglycerides were adversely associated with glaucoma in a study across three US cohorts and the UKBB.
source: In another study across three US cohorts and the UKBB, higher levels of plasma diglycerides and triglycerides were adversely associated with glaucoma (Zeleznik et al., 2023)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zeleznik et al., 2023.

claim: Hypertriglyceridemia is associated with increased blood viscosity and elevated IOP.
source: This is consistent with our observation that lower triglyceride levels were associated with glaucoma resilience, albeit with less significance compared to the three glycolysis-related metabolites. The biological mechanism is suggested to be the association of hypertriglyceridemia with increased blood viscosity and elevated IOP (Madjedi et al., 2022; Wang and Bao, 2019; Pertl et al., 2017; Rasoulinejad et al., 2015).
